title: 4 ways to rotate lifts effectively
summary: NH gives four ways to rotate lifts, from least to most structured: total freedom, choosing from a list of 15-20 lifts per body part on the day, conventional rotations triggered by failure or a set time, and his preferred autoregulated rotation. In his version, whole giant-set blocks rotate in and out of a session while specificity keeps every lift trained.

claims.claim: Switching programs too often hurts gains; change programs once every few years, while lifts can rotate every eight days.

numbers.frequency: programs every few years, lifts every 8 days

claims.claim: Method 1, total freedom (pick the body part and method on the day), isn't advised for long-term progress, but the right kind of person can still make excellent gains with it.
Method 2: keep a list of 15-20 lifts per body part and choose on the day which ones to do for the planned body parts.
On a full-body program, occasionally sneaking in a one-day body-part session when you don't feel like the plan can help free-spirited people stay consistent.
Training is always better than not training, unless you're injured.
Method 3, the most common: written rotations triggered by failure or by time (e.g. every 6 weeks). It's rigid and many have made great gains with it, though he deviates from it.
Rigid rotation feels like the program is telling you what to do; you should tell the program what to do for you.
Method 4 (his): autoregulated rotations, where you as an adult decide when a rotation happens; it punishes people who aren't consistent or dependable.
His squat day has five sections: one strength lift, then giant sets of 3-4 sets per section taking 45-50 minutes; running the whole day would take four hours.
In his rotation whole sets come in and out of a workout, sometimes skipped two weeks running, but specificity means a variation is trained elsewhere so he never detrains.
The goal of a rotation is to tire the muscle and grow, not to relearn the lift.
Autoregulated rotation takes learning, but once learned it's like riding a bike, and it combines freedom and rigidity, which makes a good program.
